domains.title: Sacred Mountain of Japan
domains.subtitle: Volcano, Pilgrimage, and National Symbol
domains.lead: Fuji is more than a mountain. For over a thousand years it has been a volcano god, a Buddhist paradise, a Shinto shrine, and the defining image of Japan. Its nearly perfect cone rises alone above the clouds, visible from the sea and from the great cities of the Kantō plain. Pilgrims have climbed it, poets have praised it, and artists have made its snow-capped form one of the most reproduced images on earth.

cards.name: Volcano Deity
cards.desc: As a living volcano, Fuji has been feared and worshipped as a source of both destruction and fertility.

cards.name: Pilgrimage Peak
cards.desc: For centuries pilgrims climbed to the summit, where shrines and lodges marked the path.

cards.name: National Symbol
cards.desc: Its image identifies Japan in art, currency, passports, and global imagination.

cards.name: Artistic Muse
cards.desc: Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views made Fuji an icon of world art.

mythology.lead: Fuji's mythology blends volcanic fear, Buddhist cosmology, and imperial symbolism. It is a mountain that generates stories because it cannot be ignored.

myths.title: The Name and Its Power
myths.text: The name Fuji is explained in folk etymology as 'without equal' (fushi) or 'inexhaustible' (fuji). The mountain was long identified with a female kami, the deity of the volcano, and with Sengen Daimyōjin, a syncretic Buddhist-Shinto figure who governed fire and fertility. Its eruptions were interpreted as the anger or fertility of the divine.

myths.title: Fuji as Lotus Mandala
myths.text: Medieval Buddhism imagined Fuji as a lotus mandala. The Fuji-kō confraternities of the Edo period climbed the mountain in white robes, reciting sutras and performing ritual circumambulations. The summit was a boundary between the human world and a Buddhist paradise, and the crater itself was sometimes identified with the Pure Land.

myths.title: The Floating World's Mountain
myths.text: Katsushika Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji and Utagawa Hiroshige's travel series fixed Fuji's image in global consciousness. It appears in calm seas, behind thunder, above villages, and through waves — always the same mountain, always changing with the viewer's place in the world.

lore.syncretism: Fuji is a palimpsest of religious traditions. Shinto Sengen shrines honor the mountain's volcanic kami; Buddhist Fuji-kō groups climbed it as a mandala; mountain ascetics (yamabushi) used it for training; and modern nationalism turned it into a symbol of the unified nation. After centuries of dormancy, its 1707 eruption reminded the capital that the sacred mountain is still alive.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fuji was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013 and remains Japan's most photographed and climbed mountain. Its image appears on banknotes, passports, and countless works of art. Each summer thousands climb through the night to greet the sunrise from the summit, continuing a pilgrimage tradition older than the nation itself.
lore.extendedMeditation: Fuji asks us to look at what endures. Cities rise and fall, governments change, but the mountain remains, altering only its cap of snow with the seasons. It is a natural fact that became a national dream.

lore.archaeology: Fuji is surrounded by Sengen shrines, of which Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha is the head. Medieval and Edo-period pilgrimage routes, lodges, and memorial stones dot the slopes and base. The 1707 Hōei eruption left extensive tephra deposits around the Edo region.
